lastPrompt: how do i turn on betterstack logging and alerting for DEV/forem alongside the existing honeybadger/datadog logging?

content.text:
You don't need any code changes. DEV runs on Heroku and Rails logs only to stdout (`config/environments/production.rb:108-115`). Datadog already gets them through a Heroku log drain, and Heroku lets an app have several drains. So you add a second drain that points at Better Stack, and Honeybadger and Datadog keep working as they do now.

**1. Create the source.** Better Stack doesn't have a DEV source yet. I checked, and the MLH team has Core, OHQ and MyMLH sources but nothing for DEV. In Telemetry, go to Sources → New → Heroku and name it something like "DEV (Heroku)". The other recent sources use the `us-west-2a` region. Copy the source token and ingesting host it gives you.

**2. Add the drain:**
```sh
heroku drains:add "https://$INGESTING_HOST:6515/events?source_token=$SOURCE_TOKEN" -a <dev-heroku-app>
heroku drains -a <dev-heroku-app>   # the Datadog drain should still be listed
```

**3. Optional: dyno metrics** for Better Stack's Heroku dashboard (memory, load, R14s):
```sh
heroku labs:enable log-runtime-metrics -a <dev-heroku-app>
```
This takes effect after the next restart or deploy.

**4. Alerting.** Better Stack alerts are built on log queries:
- Build a chart alert on a query, such as the count of `status=5\d\d` router lines, `H12`/`H13`/`R14` Heroku errors, or `ERROR` lines. Route it through an escalation policy to on-call or Slack.
- Add uptime monitors on `https://dev.to` and a health endpoint. Add heartbeats for scheduled jobs if you want them.

Before you rely on it, check three things:
- **Log level:** production defaults to `LOG_LEVEL=error` (`production.rb:65`), so Better Stack will mostly see Heroku router and platform lines plus errors, not request logs. That also keeps ingest costs down. Raising the level to `info` also raises Datadog's volume and cost.
- **Volume and cost:** the drain sends DEV's full router log stream. Check the Better Stack plan's ingest limits and retention before you turn it on.
- **Honeybadger overlap:** keep exception alerting in Honeybadger. Use Better Stack for log-pattern and platform alerts, such as H12s and memory. That also covers the retry-below-10 Sidekiq failures Honeybadger never reports.

I can set up the alerts through the Better Stack MCP once the source exists and logs are flowing. The MCP can't create sources, so step 1 has to happen in the UI.

When customizing Forem for MLH:

1. Don't edit core Forem library files (e.g. `app/models/identity.rb`) for MLH-specific behavior — put logic in MLH-owned files (`app/services/authentication/providers/mlh.rb`), inline view checks, or new files instead.
2. Don't mention "MLH Core" / Core-seeding architecture in code comments inside generalized Forem OAuth/auth code — keep such comments provider-neutral; MLH-specific comments belong only in MLH-owned files.
3. User-facing copy says "MLH", not "MyMLH" (settled 2026-08-06; `OFFICIAL_NAME` in providers/mlh.rb is the right lever).

**Why:** minimizes fork drift against upstream Forem and keeps generalized code reusable, per the repo's own re-usability philosophy.

**How to apply:** before touching a file for MLH-specific needs, ask whether it's core Forem or MLH-added (git log origin — MLH-era commits start ~#22785); prefer the MLH-owned seam. Related: [[jon-working-style]], [[dev-core-shadow-linking]].

  default_expiration = 24.hours.to_i
  config.cache_store = :redis_cache_store, { url: redis_url, expires_in: default_expiration }

  config.i18n.fallbacks = true

  config.active_support.deprecation = :notify

  config.active_support.disallowed_deprecation_warnings = []

  # Filter sensitive information from production logs
  config.filter_parameters += %i[

content.text:
---
title: Better Stack Ruby & Rails
url: /docs/logs/ruby-and-rails/
---

Where do you want to collect your Ruby logs from?

- [Rails application](#logging-from-rails)
- [Rack application](#logging-from-rack)
- [Ruby code](#logging-from-ruby)

## Logging from Rails

Collect logs from your Rails application, including your **Sidekiq jobs**. This integration also supports **Structured Events** in Rails 8.1 or higher for rich, queryable event logging.

### 1. Install

Install [Better Stack Rails Gem](https://github.com/logtail/logtail-ruby-rails):

```bash
[label Add Better Stack Rails Gem]
bundle add logtail-rails
```

### 2. Setup

Set up Better Stack Rails Gem in `config/application.rb`:

```ruby
[label config/application.rb]
module YourProject
  class Application < Rails::Application
    # ...
    # configuration of your project
    # ...

    config.logger = Logtail::Logger.create_default_logger(
      "$SOURCE_TOKEN",
      ingesting_host: "$INGESTING_HOST",
    )
  end
end
```

### 3. Start logging 🎉

Use Rails logger as usual:

```ruby
[label Send logs to Better Stack]
Rails.logger.error("Something bad happened.")
Rails.logger.warn("Log message with structured logging.", {
    item: "Orange Soda",
    price: 100.00
})

# Send a structured event (in Rails 8.1 or higher)
Rails.event.notify("user.signed_up", email: "user@example.com")
```

You should see your logs in [Better Stack Logs → Live tail](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/tail ";_blank").

Check out the [Ruby on Rails dashboard](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/dashboards/platform/ruby ";_blank").

[warning]
**Rails version 5.0 or higher is required.**  
Ruby version 2.5 or higher is required.  
[/warning]




## Logging from Rack

Collect logs from any Rack-based framework such as [Sinatra](https://sinatrarb.com), [Hanami](https://hanamirb.org), [Padrino](https://padrinorb.com), or [Roda](https://github.com/jeremyevans/roda).

### 1. Install

Install [Better Stack Rack Gem](https://github.com/logtail/logtail-ruby-rack):

```bash
[label Add Better Stack Rack Gem]
bundle add logtail-rack
```

### 2. Setup

Set up Better Stack Rack Gem in your `config.ru`:

```ruby
[label config.ru]
require 'logtail-rack'

# Initialization of logging middlewares (you don't have to use all)
use Logtail::Integrations::Rack::HTTPContext
use Logtail::Integrations::Rack::HTTPEvents
use Logtail::Integrations::Rack::ErrorEvent
use Logtail::Integrations::Rack::UserContext
use Logtail::Integrations::Rack::SessionContext

# Logger instance initialization
http_io_device = Logtail::LogDevices::HTTP.new(
  "$SOURCE_TOKEN",
  ingesting_host: "$INGESTING_HOST",
)
logger = Logtail::Logger.new(http_io_device)
Logtail::Config.instance.logger = logger

# Here is your application initialization
run ...
```

### 3. Start logging 🎉

Use the instantiated logger instance to send logs to Better Stack:

```ruby
[label Send logs to Better Stack]
logger = Logtail::Config.instance.logger

logger.info("I am using Better Stack! 🚀")

# You can also provide additional information when logging
logger.debug("Logging structured data...",
  name: {
    first: "John",
    last: "Smith"
  },
  id: 123456
)
```

You should see your logs in [Better Stack Logs → Live tail](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/tail ";_blank").


[warning]
**Rack version 1.2 or higher is required.**  
Ruby version 2.3 or higher is required.  
[/warning]




## Logging from Ruby

Collect logs from your Ruby code.

### 1. Install

Install [Better Stack Gem](https://github.com/logtail/logtail-ruby):

```bash
[label Add Better Stack Gem]
bundle add logtail
```

### 2. Setup

Set up Better Stack Ruby client:

```ruby
[label Create Better Stack logger]
require "logtail"

http_io_device = Logtail::LogDevices::HTTP.new(
  "$SOURCE_TOKEN",
  ingesting_host: "$INGESTING_HOST",
)
logger = Logtail::Logger.new(http_io_device)
```

### 3. Start logging 🎉

Use Ruby logger as usual:

```ruby
[label Send logs to Better Stack]
logger.error("Something bad happened.")
logger.warn("Log message with structured logging.", {
    item: "Orange Soda",
    price: 100.00
})

# Close logger to ensure that all logs are sent to Better Stack
logger.close
```

You should see your logs in [Better Stack → Live tail](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/tail ";_blank").

[warning]
**Ruby version 2.3.0 or higher is required.**  
[/warning]

## N+1 queries

[Bullet](https://github.com/flyerhzm/bullet) detects N+1 queries, unused eager loading, and missing counter caches in your Rails app. We'll log each detection as a structured event, tagged with the file and line that triggered it.

### 1. Install

Add the [Bullet gem](https://github.com/flyerhzm/bullet):

```
bundle add bullet
```

### 2. Configure

Enable Bullet in `config/environments/production.rb` and register a notifier that emits one structured event per detection through `Rails.logger`:

```ruby
config.after_initialize do
  Bullet.enable = true

  class BetterStackBulletNotifier < UniformNotifier::Base
    OPTIMIZATION_TYPES = {
      /\AUSE eager loading/   => "use_eager_loading",
      /\AAVOID eager loading/ => "avoid_eager_loading",
      /\ANeed Counter Cache/  => "need_counter_cache"
    }.freeze

    def self.active? = true

    def self._out_of_channel_notify(data)
      _, type = OPTIMIZATION_TYPES.find { |p, _| data[:title] =~ p }
      Rails.logger.warn(data[:title], bullet: {
        optimization_type: type,
        location: data[:body].to_s[type == "need_counter_cache" ? /\A\s*(\S.*?=>\s*\[[^\]]+\])/ : /Call stack\n  ([^\n]+)/, 1]
      })
    end
  end

  UniformNotifier.singleton_class.prepend(Module.new do
    def active_notifiers
      super + [BetterStackBulletNotifier]
    end
  end)
end
```

`BetterStackBulletNotifier` is a regular [UniformNotifier](https://github.com/flyerhzm/uniform_notifier) — the same library Bullet uses for its other output channels. It runs alongside any Bullet notifiers you already have enabled (`alert`, `console`, the in-browser footer) without affecting them.

### 3. Trigger a detection

Trigger an N+1 in your app. Open [Live tail](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/tail) and you'll see one structured event per detection:

```json
{
  "level": "warn",
  "message": "N+1 query detected",
  "bullet": {
    "optimization_type": "use_eager_loading",
    "location": "app/views/posts/index.html.erb:8:in `each'"
  }
}
```

## Sidekiq job metrics

We turn OpenTelemetry traces from Sidekiq into metrics automatically.

### 1. Install

Add the OpenTelemetry gems:

```bash
[label Add OpenTelemetry gems]
bundle add opentelemetry-sdk opentelemetry-exporter-otlp opentelemetry-instrumentation-sidekiq
```

### 2. Setup

Set up tracing in `config/initializers/opentelemetry.rb`. This initializer covers both enqueueing and processing jobs.

```ruby
[label config/initializers/opentelemetry.rb]
require "opentelemetry/sdk"
require "opentelemetry/exporter/otlp"
require "opentelemetry/instrumentation/sidekiq"

OpenTelemetry::SDK.configure do |config|
  config.resource = OpenTelemetry::SDK::Resources::Resource.create(
    "service.name" => "your-app",
  )

  config.add_span_processor(
    OpenTelemetry::SDK::Trace::Export::BatchSpanProcessor.new(
      OpenTelemetry::Exporter::OTLP::Exporter.new(
        endpoint: "https://$INGESTING_HOST/v1/traces",
        headers: { "Authorization" => "Bearer $SOURCE_TOKEN" },
        compression: "gzip",
      )
    )
  )

  config.use "OpenTelemetry::Instrumentation::Sidekiq", {
    # Name spans after the job class instead of the queue
    span_naming: :job_class,
    # Keep each job in its own trace, linked to the trace that enqueued it
    propagation_style: :link,
  }
end
```

### 3. Start tracing 🎉

Run any job. Within a couple of minutes, the data will become visible in the Sidekiq section of the [Ruby on Rails dashboard](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/dashboards/platform/ruby ";_blank").

## Need help?

Please let us know at hello@betterstack.com.  
We're happy to help! 🙏

## Example projects

You can take a look at example projects on Github:

- [Rails](https://github.com/logtail/logtail-ruby-rails)
- [Rack](https://github.com/logtail/logtail-ruby-rack)
- [Ruby](https://github.com/logtail/logtail-ruby)

## Additional information

Interested in learning more about **log levels** in Rails?  
Check out our [Intro guide to Ruby on Rails logging][how-to-start-logging-with-ruby-on-rails].

### Enrich log context

Add custom data to multiple log lines using `with` block:

[code-tabs]
```ruby
[label Rails]
Logtail.with_context(user: { id: 123 }) do
    Rails.logger.info('User logged in.')
    Rails.logger.info('User bought a gem.')
end
```
```ruby
[label Rack]
logger = Logtail::Config.instance.logger
Logtail.with_context(user: { id: 123 }) do
    logger.info('User logged in.')
    logger.info('User bought a gem.')
end
```
```ruby
[label Ruby]
Logtail.with_context(user: { id: 123 }) do
    logger.info('User logged in.')
    logger.info('User bought a gem.')
end
```
[/code-tabs]

### Filter sensitive information

In Rails or Rack, you can filter sensitive parameters and HTTP headers:

[code-tabs]
```ruby
[label Rails]
# config/initializers/filter_logging.rb
# Be sure to restart your server when you create this file.

# Configure parameters to be filtered from the log file.
# Use this to limit dissemination of sensitive information.
# See the ActiveSupport::ParameterFilter documentation for supported notations and behaviors.
Rails.application.config.filter_parameters += [
  :passw, :secret, :token, :_key, :crypt, :salt, :certificate, :otp, :ssn
]

# Configure HTTP headers to be filtered from the log.
# Use this to limit dissemination of sensitive information.
Logtail::Integrations::Rack::HTTPEvents.http_header_filters = [
  :authorization, :proxy_authorization, :cookie
]
```
```ruby
[label Rack]
# config.ru
# Be sure to restart your server when you modify this file.

# Configure HTTP headers to be filtered from the log.
# Use this to limit dissemination of sensitive information.
Logtail::Integrations::Rack::HTTPEvents.http_header_filters = [
  :authorization, :proxy_authorization, :cookie
]
```
[/code-tabs]

### Filter logs sent to Better Stack

You can prevent logger from sending certain logs to Better Stack:

[code-tabs]
```ruby
[label Rails]
# in your config/application.rb
config.logtail.filter_sent_to_better_stack do |log_entry|
    log_entry.context_snapshot[:http][:path].start_with?('/_')
end
```
```ruby
[label Rack]
```

title: Better Stack Ruby & Rails
url: /docs/logs/ruby-and-rails/

Where do you want to collect your Ruby logs from?

- [Rails application](#logging-from-rails)
- [Rack application](#logging-from-rack)
- [Ruby code](#logging-from-ruby)

## Logging from Rails

Collect logs from your Rails application, including your **Sidekiq jobs**. This integration also supports **Structured Events** in Rails 8.1 or higher for rich, queryable event logging.

### 1. Install

Install [Better Stack Rails Gem](https://github.com/logtail/logtail-ruby-rails):

```bash
[label Add Better Stack Rails Gem]
bundle add logtail-rails
```

### 2. Setup

Set up Better Stack Rails Gem in `config/application.rb`:

```ruby
[label config/application.rb]
module YourProject
  class Application < Rails::Application
    # ...
    # configuration of your project
    # ...

    config.logger = Logtail::Logger.create_default_logger(
      "$SOURCE_TOKEN",
      ingesting_host: "$INGESTING_HOST",
    )
  end
end
```

### 3. Start logging 🎉

Use Rails logger as usual:

```ruby
[label Send logs to Better Stack]
Rails.logger.error("Something bad happened.")
Rails.logger.warn("Log message with structured logging.", {
    item: "Orange Soda",
    price: 100.00
})

# Send a structured event (in Rails 8.1 or higher)
Rails.event.notify("user.signed_up", email: "user@example.com")
```

You should see your logs in [Better Stack Logs → Live tail](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/tail ";_blank").

Check out the [Ruby on Rails dashboard](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/dashboards/platform/ruby ";_blank").

[warning]
**Rails version 5.0 or higher is required.**  
Ruby version 2.5 or higher is required.  
[/warning]




## Logging from Rack

Collect logs from any Rack-based framework such as [Sinatra](https://sinatrarb.com), [Hanami](https://hanamirb.org), [Padrino](https://padrinorb.com), or [Roda](https://github.com/jeremyevans/roda).

### 1. Install

Install [Better Stack Rack Gem](https://github.com/logtail/logtail-ruby-rack):

```bash
[label Add Better Stack Rack Gem]
bundle add logtail-rack
```

### 2. Setup

Set up Better Stack Rack Gem in your `config.ru`:

```ruby
[label config.ru]
require 'logtail-rack'

# Initialization of logging middlewares (you don't have to use all)
use Logtail::Integrations::Rack::HTTPContext
use Logtail::Integrations::Rack::HTTPEvents
use Logtail::Integrations::Rack::ErrorEvent
use Logtail::Integrations::Rack::UserContext
use Logtail::Integrations::Rack::SessionContext

# Logger instance initialization
http_io_device = Logtail::LogDevices::HTTP.new(
  "$SOURCE_TOKEN",
  ingesting_host: "$INGESTING_HOST",
)
logger = Logtail::Logger.new(http_io_device)
Logtail::Config.instance.logger = logger

# Here is your application initialization
run ...
```

### 3. Start logging 🎉

Use the instantiated logger instance to send logs to Better Stack:

```ruby
[label Send logs to Better Stack]
logger = Logtail::Config.instance.logger

logger.info("I am using Better Stack! 🚀")

# You can also provide additional information when logging
logger.debug("Logging structured data...",
  name: {
    first: "John",
    last: "Smith"
  },
  id: 123456
)
```

You should see your logs in [Better Stack Logs → Live tail](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/tail ";_blank").


[warning]
**Rack version 1.2 or higher is required.**  
Ruby version 2.3 or higher is required.  
[/warning]




## Logging from Ruby

Collect logs from your Ruby code.

### 1. Install

Install [Better Stack Gem](https://github.com/logtail/logtail-ruby):

```bash
[label Add Better Stack Gem]
bundle add logtail
```

### 2. Setup

Set up Better Stack Ruby client:

```ruby
[label Create Better Stack logger]
require "logtail"

http_io_device = Logtail::LogDevices::HTTP.new(
  "$SOURCE_TOKEN",
  ingesting_host: "$INGESTING_HOST",
)
logger = Logtail::Logger.new(http_io_device)
```

### 3. Start logging 🎉

Use Ruby logger as usual:

```ruby
[label Send logs to Better Stack]
logger.error("Something bad happened.")
logger.warn("Log message with structured logging.", {
    item: "Orange Soda",
    price: 100.00
})

# Close logger to ensure that all logs are sent to Better Stack
logger.close
```

You should see your logs in [Better Stack → Live tail](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/tail ";_blank").

[warning]
**Ruby version 2.3.0 or higher is required.**  
[/warning]

## N+1 queries

[Bullet](https://github.com/flyerhzm/bullet) detects N+1 queries, unused eager loading, and missing counter caches in your Rails app. We'll log each detection as a structured event, tagged with the file and line that triggered it.

### 1. Install

Add the [Bullet gem](https://github.com/flyerhzm/bullet):

```
bundle add bullet
```

### 2. Configure

Enable Bullet in `config/environments/production.rb` and register a notifier that emits one structured event per detection through `Rails.logger`:

```ruby
config.after_initialize do
  Bullet.enable = true

  class BetterStackBulletNotifier < UniformNotifier::Base
    OPTIMIZATION_TYPES = {
      /\AUSE eager loading/   => "use_eager_loading",
      /\AAVOID eager loading/ => "avoid_eager_loading",
      /\ANeed Counter Cache/  => "need_counter_cache"
    }.freeze

    def self.active? = true

    def self._out_of_channel_notify(data)
      _, type = OPTIMIZATION_TYPES.find { |p, _| data[:title] =~ p }
      Rails.logger.warn(data[:title], bullet: {
        optimization_type: type,
        location: data[:body].to_s[type == "need_counter_cache" ? /\A\s*(\S.*?=>\s*\[[^\]]+\])/ : /Call stack\n  ([^\n]+)/, 1]
      })
    end
  end

  UniformNotifier.singleton_class.prepend(Module.new do
    def active_notifiers
      super + [BetterStackBulletNotifier]
    end
  end)
end
```

`BetterStackBulletNotifier` is a regular [UniformNotifier](https://github.com/flyerhzm/uniform_notifier) — the same library Bullet uses for its other output channels. It runs alongside any Bullet notifiers you already have enabled (`alert`, `console`, the in-browser footer) without affecting them.

### 3. Trigger a detection

Trigger an N+1 in your app. Open [Live tail](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/tail) and you'll see one structured event per detection:

```json
{
  "level": "warn",
  "message": "N+1 query detected",
  "bullet": {
    "optimization_type": "use_eager_loading",
    "location": "app/views/posts/index.html.erb:8:in `each'"
  }
}
```

## Sidekiq job metrics

We turn OpenTelemetry traces from Sidekiq into metrics automatically.

### 1. Install

Add the OpenTelemetry gems:

```bash
[label Add OpenTelemetry gems]
bundle add opentelemetry-sdk opentelemetry-exporter-otlp opentelemetry-instrumentation-sidekiq
```

### 2. Setup

Set up tracing in `config/initializers/opentelemetry.rb`. This initializer covers both enqueueing and processing jobs.

```ruby
[label config/initializers/opentelemetry.rb]
require "opentelemetry/sdk"
require "opentelemetry/exporter/otlp"
require "opentelemetry/instrumentation/sidekiq"

OpenTelemetry::SDK.configure do |config|
  config.resource = OpenTelemetry::SDK::Resources::Resource.create(
    "service.name" => "your-app",
  )

  config.add_span_processor(
    OpenTelemetry::SDK::Trace::Export::BatchSpanProcessor.new(
      OpenTelemetry::Exporter::OTLP::Exporter.new(
        endpoint: "https://$INGESTING_HOST/v1/traces",
        headers: { "Authorization" => "Bearer $SOURCE_TOKEN" },
        compression: "gzip",
      )
    )
  )

  config.use "OpenTelemetry::Instrumentation::Sidekiq", {
    # Name spans after the job class instead of the queue
    span_naming: :job_class,
    # Keep each job in its own trace, linked to the trace that enqueued it
    propagation_style: :link,
  }
end
```

### 3. Start tracing 🎉

Run any job. Within a couple of minutes, the data will become visible in the Sidekiq section of the [Ruby on Rails dashboard](https://telemetry.betterstack.com/team/0/dashboards/platform/ruby ";_blank").

def self.create_default_logger(source_token, options = {})
      # Handle backward-compatibility of argument names from v0.2.9
      options[:ingesting_host] ||= options[:telemetry_host] if options[:telemetry_host].present?
      options[:ingesting_port] ||= options[:telemetry_port] if options[:telemetry_port].present?
      options[:ingesting_scheme] ||= options[:telemetry_scheme] if options[:telemetry_scheme].present?

      if ENV['LOGTAIL_SKIP_LOGS'].blank? && !Rails.env.test?
        io_device = Logtail::LogDevices::HTTP.new(source_token, options)
      else
        io_device = STDOUT
      end

      logger = self.create_logger(io_device)

      if defined?(Sidekiq)
        require "logtail-rails/sidekiq"

        Sidekiq.configure_server do |config|
          logger = self.create_logger(io_device, config.logger) if config.logger.class == Sidekiq::Logger
          config.logger = logger
        end
      end

      # For Rails 8.1 and above, subscribe to the event system
      Rails.event.subscribe(Logtail::Integrations::Rails::EventLogSubscriber.new(logger)) if Rails.respond_to?(:event)

      logger
    end
  end
end

You are an expert ClickHouse query generator for telemetry data. Generate ONLY valid SQL queries following these strict rules.

> **This tool is for queries run directly (e.g., via `query` or `render_chart`).** If the query will be saved as a dashboard chart or chart alert, stop and use `metrics_query_help` with `context: 'chart_query'` instead — dashboard charts always query the metrics collection (the server auto-converts `{{source}}` to the metrics collection for any source type, including logs/spans), so `JSONExtract(raw, …)` against a chart's `{{source}}` will not work. For raw-log fields in a chart, use a live-tail chart (`chart_type: 'tail_chart'`).

## DATA SOURCES AND HOW TO USE THEM

### Available Tables and Collections

Table name              | Collection name                                | Description                                                                                             | Sample query                                                                                                                            
----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
t150729.dev_to_heroku_2 | remote(t150729_dev_to_heroku_2_logs)           | Recent logs data (hot storage)                                                                          | SELECT dt, raw FROM remote(t150729_dev_to_heroku_2_logs) LIMIT 10                                                                       
t150729.dev_to_heroku_2 | s3Cluster(primary, t150729_dev_to_heroku_2_s3) | Historical logs data. Use `_row_type = 1 /* logs */` to filter the result and get only logs.            | SELECT dt, raw FROM s3Cluster(primary, t150729_dev_to_heroku_2_s3) WHERE _row_type = 1 /* logs */ LIMIT 10                              
t150729.dev_to_heroku_2 | remote(t150729_dev_to_heroku_2_spans)          | Recent tracing spans data                                                                               | SELECT dt, raw FROM remote(t150729_dev_to_heroku_2_spans) LIMIT 10                                                                      
t150729.dev_to_heroku_2 | s3Cluster(primary, t150729_dev_to_heroku_2_s3) | Historical tracing spans data. Use `_row_type = 3 /* spans */` to filter the result and get only spans. | SELECT dt, raw FROM s3Cluster(primary, t150729_dev_to_heroku_2_s3) WHERE _row_type = 3 /* spans */ LIMIT 10                             
t150729.dev_to_heroku_2 | remote(t150729_dev_to_heroku_2_metrics)        | Pre-aggregated counters and metrics. Retains far longer than the ~30 minute hot window.                 | SELECT toStartOfHour(dt) AS time, sum(logs_count) FROM remote(t150729_dev_to_heroku_2_metrics) GROUP BY time ORDER BY time DESC LIMIT 10

Notes:
- The collection names are following the pattern: `t<team_id>_<source_slug>_<type>`, e.g. `t123_source1_logs` or `t123_source2_s3`

### Understanding Collections vs Tables

**IMPORTANT**: The "Collection name" is what you use in the FROM clause, NOT the table name!
**IMPORTANT**: You should ALWAYS use one of the two functions (`remote()` or `s3Cluster()`) to access data, NEVER use the table name directly!

- **remote()** function: Accesses recent/hot data — **only the last ~30 minutes**
  - Fast queries for events from the last few minutes
  - Empty result ≠ "no data": if your time range reaches further back than ~30 minutes, the rows are in S3 (see below), not here
  - Example: `FROM remote(t123_source1_logs)`

- **s3Cluster()** function: Accesses historical/cold data from object storage — **everything older than ~30 minutes**
  - The default choice for any range longer than ~30 minutes, or any time you're unsure. To cover a window that runs up to "now", `UNION ALL` the recent collection with S3.
  - The s3 table is a fan-in across every row type, so it MUST be filtered down to yours: `WHERE _row_type = 1 /* logs */`. Copy that filter verbatim; it is the only row type this source needs.
  - Example: `FROM s3Cluster(primary, t123_source2_s3)`

- Counting events over a long range? Neither of the above. The **metrics** collection listed in the table above holds a pre-aggregated per-row-type counter and keeps far more than ~30 minutes, so `sum(logs_count)` / `sum(spans_count)` over it beats scanning raw rows, needs no `_row_type` filter, and needs no hot/cold union.

**IMPORTANT**: When asked for the table name, always include the full table name, so `t123.shop`, instead of just `shop` or `t123``

### Data Structure

**Main columns in logs/spans tables:**
- `dt` (DateTime) - Timestamp of the event (use for time filtering)
- `_pattern` (String) - Pattern for grouping similar logs (dynamic values like IDs/numbers are stripped)
  - Example: Log message "User 123 updated post 456" becomes pattern "User ? updated post ?"
  - Use `GROUP BY _pattern` to find logs with the same structure regardless of specific IDs
  - Perfect for finding patterns like "all user update events" or "all database connection errors"
- `raw` (String) - JSON payload containing all the actual log/span data
- `_row_type` - Row type identifier. A plain `UInt8` on the s3 table, where `_row_type = 1 /* logs */` is the filter for this source; an `Enum8` filtered by name (`'log'`, `'metric'`, `'span'`, `'exception'`, `'event'`, `'replay'`, `'extracted_metric'`, `'web_event'`) on the metrics collection; absent from the per-type hot collections, which need no filter

**All actual log/span fields are inside the `raw` JSON column!**

### Available fields in the raw JSON

Path | Type
--- | ---
'context', 'release', 'commit_hash' | String
'context', 'release', 'created_at' | String
'context', 'runtime', 'file' | String
'context', 'runtime', 'frame_label' | String
'context', 'runtime', 'line' | Int64
'context', 'runtime', 'thread_id' | Int64
'context', 'system', 'hostname' | String
'context', 'system', 'pid' | Int64
'dt' | String
'level' | String
'message' | String
'tags' | Array(Nullable(String))

## JSON DATA EXTRACTION

### Extracting Fields from raw JSON

Use `JSONExtract` to access fields inside the `raw` column:

```sql
-- Top-level fields
JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS log_level
JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)') AS message
JSONExtract(raw, 'timestamp', 'Nullable(DateTime)') AS event_time

-- Nested fields (use separate arguments for each level)
JSONExtract(raw, 'metadata', 'user_id', 'Nullable(Int32)') AS user_id
JSONExtract(raw, 'error', 'code', 'Nullable(Int32)') AS error_code
JSONExtract(raw, 'request', 'headers', 'user-agent', 'Nullable(String)') AS user_agent

-- Fields with dots in their names (treat as single field name)
JSONExtract(raw, 'field.with.dots', 'Nullable(String)') AS dotted_field
```

### CRITICAL: Always Use Nullable Types
- ALWAYS wrap types with `Nullable()`: `Nullable(String)`, `Nullable(Int32)`, etc.
- This prevents query failures when fields are missing
- ✅ CORRECT: `JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)')`
- ❌ WRONG: `JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'String')`

## QUERY BEST PRACTICES

### Essential Rules
1. **Always use LIMIT** - Prevent fetching too much data accidentally
2. **Order your results** - Use `ORDER BY dt DESC` or `ORDER BY dt ASC` for consistent results
3. **Filter early** - Apply WHERE conditions to reduce data scanned
4. **Size time ranges by rows, not by width** - see 'Query budget' below
5. **Filter NULL values** - Add `IS NOT NULL` checks after extracting JSON fields

### Query budget

One `query` call reads at most 50,000,000 rows from S3 and is stopped after 60 seconds. Before running an `s3Cluster(...)` query the tool counts the rows its `dt` filter covers; over the budget it refuses without scanning and returns time windows that fit, which you run one by one and merge yourself (rows concatenate; `count()` and `sum()` add up; `min()` and `max()` combine; an average needs `sum()` and `count()` per window; `quantile(...)`, `uniq(...)` and `count(DISTINCT ...)` do not merge, keep those to one window). Keep the time filter on the bare `dt` column so the tool can size it; a query it cannot size runs unguarded, and the 60-second stop still applies. To measure a range yourself, sum the source's `_metrics` collection counter (`logs_count`, `spans_count`, `exceptions_count` or `replays_count`) per `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 30 MINUTE)`: one cheap query.

### SQL formatting

Format queries with each top-level clause keyword (`SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`, `HAVING`, `LIMIT`) on its own line and the clause body indented two spaces. Put each selected expression, filter, grouping term, or sort key on its own line. Example:

```sql
SELECT
  {{time}} AS time,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS series,
  count() AS value
FROM
  {{source}}
WHERE
  dt BETWEEN {{start_time}} AND {{end_time}}
GROUP BY
  time,
  series
ORDER BY
  time
```

### Aggregation Functions
Use standard aggregation functions (NOT Merge variants):
- `count(*)`, `count(DISTINCT ...)`
- `avg(...)`, `sum(...)`, `min(...)`, `max(...)`
- `any(...)`, `anyLast(...)`
- `groupArray(...)`, `quantile(...)`

## PRACTICAL QUERY EXAMPLES

### Query Recent Logs (Last 30 minutes)
```sql
SELECT
  dt,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)') AS message,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'service', 'Nullable(String)') AS service
FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
WHERE dt > now() - INTERVAL 30 MINUTE
ORDER BY dt DESC
LIMIT 100
```

### Query Historical Logs (Older than 30 minutes)
```sql
SELECT
  dt,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)') AS message
FROM s3Cluster(primary, db_123_table_s3)
WHERE
  _row_type = 1 /* logs */  -- Critical: read only this source's own rows
  AND dt BETWEEN now() - INTERVAL 7 DAY AND now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
  AND JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') = 'error'
ORDER BY dt DESC
LIMIT 100
```

### Combine Recent and Historical Data
```sql
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT
    dt,
    JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
    JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)') AS message
  FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
  WHERE dt > now() - INTERVAL 24 HOUR

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    dt,
    JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
    JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)') AS message
  FROM s3Cluster(primary, db_123_table_s3)
  WHERE
    _row_type = 1 /* logs */
    AND dt > now() - INTERVAL 24 HOUR
)
ORDER BY dt DESC
LIMIT 100
```

### Count Errors by Service (Aggregation)
```sql
WITH
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'service', 'Nullable(String)') AS service
SELECT
  service,
  count(*) AS error_count
FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
WHERE
  dt > now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR
  AND level = 'error'
  AND service IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY error_count DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Find Slow API Requests
```sql
SELECT
  dt,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'request', 'path', 'Nullable(String)') AS endpoint,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'duration_ms', 'Nullable(Float64)') AS duration,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'user', 'id', 'Nullable(String)') AS user_id
FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
WHERE
  dt > now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR
  AND JSONExtract(raw, 'duration_ms', 'Nullable(Float64)') > 1000
  AND JSONExtract(raw, 'request', 'path', 'Nullable(String)') LIKE '/api/%'
ORDER BY duration DESC
LIMIT 50
```

### Time Series Aggregation (Logs per Minute)
```sql
SELECT
  toStartOfMinute(dt) AS minute,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
  count(*) AS count
FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
WHERE dt > now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR
GROUP BY minute, level
ORDER BY minute DESC, level
```

### Group Similar Logs by Pattern
```sql
SELECT
  _pattern,
  count(*) AS occurrence_count,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
  any(JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)')) AS example_message
FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
WHERE
  dt > now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR
  AND JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') = 'error'
GROUP BY _pattern, level
ORDER BY occurrence_count DESC
LIMIT 20
```

## OUTPUT REQUIREMENTS

Return ONLY the SQL query. No explanations, no XML tags, no markdown code blocks, no comments.

```sql
JSONExtract(raw, 'request', 'headers', 'user-agent', 'Nullable(String)') AS user_agent

-- Fields with dots in their names (treat as single field name)
JSONExtract(raw, 'field.with.dots', 'Nullable(String)') AS dotted_field
```

### CRITICAL: Always Use Nullable Types
- ALWAYS wrap types with `Nullable()`: `Nullable(String)`, `Nullable(Int32)`, etc.
- This prevents query failures when fields are missing
- ✅ CORRECT: `JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)')`
- ❌ WRONG: `JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'String')`

## QUERY BEST PRACTICES

### Essential Rules
1. **Always use LIMIT** - Prevent fetching too much data accidentally
2. **Order your results** - Use `ORDER BY dt DESC` or `ORDER BY dt ASC` for consistent results
3. **Filter early** - Apply WHERE conditions to reduce data scanned
4. **Size time ranges by rows, not by width** - see 'Query budget' below
5. **Filter NULL values** - Add `IS NOT NULL` checks after extracting JSON fields

### Query budget

One `query` call reads at most 50,000,000 rows from S3 and is stopped after 60 seconds. Before running an `s3Cluster(...)` query the tool counts the rows its `dt` filter covers; over the budget it refuses without scanning and returns time windows that fit, which you run one by one and merge yourself (rows concatenate; `count()` and `sum()` add up; `min()` and `max()` combine; an average needs `sum()` and `count()` per window; `quantile(...)`, `uniq(...)` and `count(DISTINCT ...)` do not merge, keep those to one window). Keep the time filter on the bare `dt` column so the tool can size it; a query it cannot size runs unguarded, and the 60-second stop still applies. To measure a range yourself, sum the source's `_metrics` collection counter (`logs_count`, `spans_count`, `exceptions_count` or `replays_count`) per `toStartOfInterval(dt, INTERVAL 30 MINUTE)`: one cheap query.

### SQL formatting

Format queries with each top-level clause keyword (`SELECT`, `FROM`, `WHERE`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`, `HAVING`, `LIMIT`) on its own line and the clause body indented two spaces. Put each selected expression, filter, grouping term, or sort key on its own line. Example:

```sql
SELECT
  {{time}} AS time,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS series,
  count() AS value
FROM
  {{source}}
WHERE
  dt BETWEEN {{start_time}} AND {{end_time}}
GROUP BY
  time,
  series
ORDER BY
  time
```

### Aggregation Functions
Use standard aggregation functions (NOT Merge variants):
- `count(*)`, `count(DISTINCT ...)`
- `avg(...)`, `sum(...)`, `min(...)`, `max(...)`
- `any(...)`, `anyLast(...)`
- `groupArray(...)`, `quantile(...)`

## PRACTICAL QUERY EXAMPLES

### Query Recent Logs (Last 30 minutes)
```sql
SELECT
  dt,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)') AS message,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'service', 'Nullable(String)') AS service
FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
WHERE dt > now() - INTERVAL 30 MINUTE
ORDER BY dt DESC
LIMIT 100
```

### Query Historical Logs (Older than 30 minutes)
```sql
SELECT
  dt,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)') AS message
FROM s3Cluster(primary, db_123_table_s3)
WHERE
  _row_type = 1 /* logs */  -- Critical: read only this source's own rows
  AND dt BETWEEN now() - INTERVAL 7 DAY AND now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
  AND JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') = 'error'
ORDER BY dt DESC
LIMIT 100
```

### Combine Recent and Historical Data
```sql
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT
    dt,
    JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
    JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)') AS message
  FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
  WHERE dt > now() - INTERVAL 24 HOUR

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    dt,
    JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
    JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)') AS message
  FROM s3Cluster(primary, db_123_table_s3)
  WHERE
    _row_type = 1 /* logs */
    AND dt > now() - INTERVAL 24 HOUR
)
ORDER BY dt DESC
LIMIT 100
```

### Count Errors by Service (Aggregation)
```sql
WITH
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'service', 'Nullable(String)') AS service
SELECT
  service,
  count(*) AS error_count
FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
WHERE
  dt > now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR
  AND level = 'error'
  AND service IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY error_count DESC
LIMIT 10
```

### Find Slow API Requests
```sql
SELECT
  dt,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'request', 'path', 'Nullable(String)') AS endpoint,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'duration_ms', 'Nullable(Float64)') AS duration,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'user', 'id', 'Nullable(String)') AS user_id
FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
WHERE
  dt > now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR
  AND JSONExtract(raw, 'duration_ms', 'Nullable(Float64)') > 1000
  AND JSONExtract(raw, 'request', 'path', 'Nullable(String)') LIKE '/api/%'
ORDER BY duration DESC
LIMIT 50
```

### Time Series Aggregation (Logs per Minute)
```sql
SELECT
  toStartOfMinute(dt) AS minute,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
  count(*) AS count
FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
WHERE dt > now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR
GROUP BY minute, level
ORDER BY minute DESC, level
```

### Group Similar Logs by Pattern
```sql
SELECT
  _pattern,
  count(*) AS occurrence_count,
  JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') AS level,
  any(JSONExtract(raw, 'message', 'Nullable(String)')) AS example_message
FROM remote(db_123_table_logs)
WHERE
  dt > now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR
  AND JSONExtract(raw, 'level', 'Nullable(String)') = 'error'
GROUP BY _pattern, level
ORDER BY occurrence_count DESC
LIMIT 20
```

Return ONLY the SQL query. No explanations, no XML tags, no markdown code blocks, no comments.

            config.app_middleware.use middleware_class

require "active_support/core_ext/integer/time"

# rubocop:disable Metrics/BlockLength
Rails.application.configure do
  # Allow the app to know when booted up in context where we haven't set ENV vars
  # If we have not set this ENV var it means we haven't set the environment
  ENV["ENV_AVAILABLE"] = ENV["APP_DOMAIN"].present?.to_s

  if ENV["ENV_AVAILABLE"] == "false"
    # We still need _something_ here, but if booted without environment (aka asset precompile),
    # it shouldn't need to be the proper value
    ENV["SECRET_KEY_BASE"] = "NOT_SET"
  end

  # Configure secret_key_base directly from environment variable to support Rails 7.2 and 8.0
  config.secret_key_base = ENV["SECRET_KEY_BASE"]
  # Settings specified here will take precedence over those in config/application.rb.

  # Code is not reloaded between requests.
  config.enable_reloading = false

  # Eager load code on boot. This eager loads most of Rails and
  # your application in memory, allowing both threaded web servers
  # and those relying on copy on write to perform better.
  # Rake tasks automatically ignore this option for performance.
  config.eager_load = true

  # Full error reports are disabled and caching is turned on.
  config.consider_all_requests_local       = false
  config.action_controller.perform_caching = true

  # Ensures that a master key has been made available in either ENV["RAILS_MASTER_KEY"]
  # or in config/master.key. This key is used to decrypt credentials (and other encrypted files).
  # config.require_master_key = true

  # Disable serving static files from the `/public` folder by default since
  # Apache or NGINX already handles this.
  config.public_file_server.enabled = ENV["RAILS_SERVE_STATIC_FILES"].present?
  config.public_file_server.headers = {
    "Cache-Control" => "public, s-maxage=#{30.days.to_i}, max-age=#{3000.days.to_i}"
  }

  # Compress JavaScripts and CSS.
  config.assets.js_compressor = :terser
  # config.assets.css_compressor = :sass

  # Do not fallback to assets pipeline if a precompiled asset is missed.
  config.assets.compile = true

  # `config.assets.precompile` and `config.assets.version` have moved to config/initializers/assets.rb
  config.assets.digest = true

  # Enable serving of images, stylesheets, and JavaScripts from an asset server.
  config.action_controller.asset_host = ENV.fetch("FASTLY_CDN_URL", nil)

  # Specifies the header that your server uses for sending files.
  # config.action_dispatch.x_sendfile_header = 'X-Sendfile' # for Apache
  # config.action_dispatch.x_sendfile_header = 'X-Accel-Redirect' # for NGINX

  # Force all access to the app over SSL, use Strict-Transport-Security, and use secure cookies.
  config.force_ssl = ENV["FORCE_SSL_IN_RAILS"] == "true"

  # Use the lowest log level to ensure availability of diagnostic information
  # when problems arise.
  config.log_level = ENV.fetch("LOG_LEVEL", :error)

  # Prepend all log lines with the following tags.
  config.log_tags = [:request_id]

  # We have the option of a secondary cache store, but it is not required.
  # The secondary store could be used for redundancy or to be used for swapping stores.
  redis_url = ENV.fetch("REDISCLOUD_URL", nil)
  redis_url ||= ENV.fetch("REDIS_URL", nil)
  default_expiration = 24.hours.to_i
  config.cache_store = :redis_cache_store, { url: redis_url, expires_in: default_expiration }

  config.action_mailer.perform_caching = false

  # Ignore bad email addresses and do not raise email delivery errors.
  # Set this to true and configure the email server for immediate delivery to raise delivery errors.
  # config.action_mailer.raise_delivery_errors = false

  # Enable locale fallbacks for I18n (makes lookups for any locale fall back to
  # the I18n.default_locale when a translation cannot be found).
  config.i18n.fallbacks = true

  # Send deprecation notices to registered listeners.
  config.active_support.deprecation = :notify

  # Log disallowed deprecations.
  config.active_support.disallowed_deprecation = :log

  # Tell Active Support which deprecation messages to disallow.
  config.active_support.disallowed_deprecation_warnings = []

  # Filter sensitive information from production logs
  config.filter_parameters += %i[
    auth_data_dump content email encrypted
    encrypted_password message_html message_markdown
    password previous_refresh_token refresh_token secret
    to token current_sign_in_ip last_sign_in_ip
    reset_password_token remember_token unconfirmed_email
  ]

  # Use default logging formatter so that PID and timestamp are not suppressed.
  config.log_formatter = Logger::Formatter.new

  if ENV["RAILS_LOG_TO_STDOUT"].present?
    # Use a different logger for distributed setups.
    # require 'syslog/logger'
    # config.logger = ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging.new(Syslog::Logger.new 'app-name')

    logger           = ActiveSupport::Logger.new($stdout)
    logger.formatter = config.log_formatter
    config.logger    = ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging.new(logger)
  end

  if ENV["BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN"].present?
    betterstack_logger = Logtail::Logger.create_default_logger(
      ENV["BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN"],
      ingesting_host: ENV.fetch("BETTERSTACK_INGESTING_HOST", nil),
    )
    config.logger = ActiveSupport::BroadcastLogger.new(*[config.logger, betterstack_logger].compact)
  end

  config.active_record.dump_schema_after_migration = false

  config.action_mailer.perform_deliveries = false
  config.action_mailer.default_url_options = { host: protocol + ENV["APP_DOMAIN"].to_s }

#   ensuring you do not lose log data, pass a standard {SizedQueue}. See examples for
      #   an example.
      # @option attributes [Symbol] :ingesting_host The Better Stack Telemetry ingesting host to delivery the log lines to.
      #   The default is set via {INGESTING_HOST}.
      #
      # @example Basic usage
      #   Logtail::Logger.new(Logtail::LogDevices::HTTP.new("<source_token>", ingesting_host: "<ingesting_host>"))
      #
      # @example Apply back pressure instead of dropping messages
      #   http_log_device = Logtail::LogDevices::HTTP.new("<source_token>", ingesting_host: "<ingesting_host>", request_queue: SizedQueue.new(25))
      #   Logtail::Logger.new(http_log_device)
      def initialize(source_token, options = {})
        # Handle backward-compatibility of argument names
        options[:ingesting_host] ||= options[:logtail_host]
        options[:ingesting_port] ||= options[:logtail_port]
        options[:ingesting_scheme] ||= options[:logtail_scheme]

        @source_token = source_token || raise(ArgumentError.new("The source_token parameter cannot be blank"))
        @ingesting_host = options[:ingesting_host] || ENV['INGESTING_HOST'] || ENV['LOGTAIL_HOST'] || DEFAULT_INGESTING_HOST
        @ingesting_port = options[:ingesting_port] || ENV['INGESTING_PORT'] || ENV['LOGTAIL_PORT'] || DEFAULT_INGESTING_PORT
        @ingesting_scheme = options[:ingesting_scheme] || ENV['INGESTING_SCHEME'] || ENV['LOGTAIL_SCHEME'] || DEFAULT_INGESTING_SCHEME
        @batch_size = options[:batch_size] || 1_000
        @flush_continuously = options[:flush_continuously] != false
        @flush_interval = options[:flush_interval] || 2 # 2 seconds
        @requests_per_conn = options[:requests_per_conn] || 2_500
        @msg_queue = FlushableDroppingSizedQueue.new(@batch_size)
        @request_queue = options[:request_queue] || FlushableDroppingSizedQueue.new(25)
        @successive_error_count = 0
        @requests_in_flight = 0
      end

      # Write a new log line message to the buffer, and flush asynchronously if the
      # message queue is full. We flush asynchronously because the maximum message batch
      # size is constricted by the Logtail API. The actual application limit is a multiple
      # of this. Hence the `@request_queue`.
      def write(msg)
        return unless Logtail.config.send_to_better_stack?(msg)

        @msg_queue.enq(msg)

        # Lazily start flush threads to ensure threads are alive after forking processes.
        # If the threads are started during instantiation they will not be copied when
        # the current process is forked. This is the case with various web servers,
        # such as phusion passenger.
        ensure_flush_threads_are_started

        if @msg_queue.full?
          Logtail::Config.instance.debug { "Flushing HTTP buffer via write" }
          flush_async
        end
        true
      end

      # Flush all log messages in the buffer synchronously. This method will not return
      # until delivery of the messages has been successful. If you want to flush
      # asynchronously see {#flush_async}.
      def flush
        flush_async
        wait_on_request_queue
        true
      end

      # Closes the log device, cleans up, and attempts one last delivery.
      def close
        # Kill the flush thread immediately since we are about to flush again.
        @flush_thread.kill if @flush_thread

        # Flush all remaining messages
        flush

        # Kill the request queue thread. Flushing ensures that no requests are pending.
        @request_outlet_thread.kill if @request_outlet_thread
      end

      def deliver_one(msg)
        http = build_http

content.text:
DEV's Rails logs are set up to go to Better Stack as well as stdout, so the Datadog drain is untouched. It stays off until you set two config vars. I sent test lines with your token, and they showed up in the "DEV.to (Heroku)" source (id 2773094).

**To turn it on:** I haven't changed prod myself. Setting the vars restarts the dynos:
```sh
heroku config:set REDACTED \
  BETTERSTACK_INGESTING_HOST=s2773094.eu-central-1a.betterstackdata.com -a <dev-app>
```
The token isn't in the code. Other Forem installs, dev and test are unaffected unless the token is set.

**Changes** (not committed):
- **`Gemfile`, `Gemfile.lock`, `vendor/cache/logtail-0.1.17.gem`:** adds `logtail` with `require: false`.
- **`config/environments/production.rb:118-130`:** when the token is set, Rails logs go to both stdout and Better Stack.

**Where I departed from the guide:**
- **Not `logtail-rails`:** loading that gem patches `TaggedLogging`, swaps Rails' request and controller log subscribers, and adds 5 Rack middlewares. That happens on every boot, whether or not the token is set, and would change what Datadog sees. The same guide's plain-Ruby `logtail` gem has none of those patches.
- **Not `config.logger = …` in `application.rb`:** that would replace the stdout logger, and Datadog would lose Rails logs. It would also be overridden anyway, because `production.rb` sets its own logger afterwards.
- **I avoided a bug that would have run every job twice:** my first version gave both loggers tag support, and the test showed tagged log blocks running once per logger. ActiveJob runs every job inside one of those blocks. The Better Stack logger now has no tag support, and I confirmed the block runs once and each line arrives once.

**What you'll see in Better Stack:**
- **Errors only:** prod's `LOG_LEVEL` defaults to `error`, so that's all that ships.
- **No request_id:** stdout keeps its `[request_id]` tags, but Better Stack entries won't have them.
- **Most Sidekiq output stays on stdout:** Sidekiq's own start/done/fail lines only go to stdout. Anything workers log through `Rails.logger` does reach Better Stack.
- **No router or platform lines:** Heroku router lines (H12, R14) only reach Better Stack through the log drain from my earlier message.
- **Test lines:** the source now holds a few test lines from my laptop (`Mac.localdomain`).

content.text:
No. Every log line at `error` level or above goes to Better Stack. The only filter is `LOG_LEVEL`.

Under heavy load it can still lose lines. The Logtail HTTP device batches up to 1,000 lines per request and flushes every 2 seconds. It keeps at most 25 requests waiting to send, and when that queue is full it silently drops new batches instead of blocking. So during an error storm, or if Better Stack is slow, some lines never arrive and nothing tells you. For alerting that's usually fine, because a storm still crosses any threshold. Just don't treat Better Stack counts as exact during those periods.

The other systems:
- **Datadog:** logs come through the Heroku drain and aren't sampled. APM spans are sampled, but the trace metrics count every request, so they're exact.
- **Honeybadger:** no sampling, but it has two gaps. It ignores some exceptions (for example `RateLimitChecker::LimitReached` in `config/initializers/honeybadger.rb`). It also never reports failures from Sidekiq jobs that retry fewer than 10 times.

If you'd rather slow the app down than drop lines, pass `request_queue: SizedQueue.new(25)` to `HTTP.new`. It's a one-line change, but if Better Stack goes down, logging calls block and the app stalls. I'd keep the dropping behaviour.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

author: jonmarkgo
files: Gemfile, Gemfile.lock, config/initializers/opentelemetry.rb, config/initializers/sentry.rb
comments: 0
---
## Observability pilot: env-gated Better Stack errors + sampled OpenTelemetry tracing

Adds two **completely inert-by-default** observability integrations. Nothing changes
behavior unless the new env vars are set, and they are **set nowhere yet**.

### Runs ALONGSIDE the existing stack (neither is touched)
- **Honeybadger** stays the alerting **source of truth** for errors. Sentry SDK is added
  *in addition*, shipping the same errors to Better Stack via its Sentry-protocol ingest.
  `config/initializers/honeybadger.rb` is unchanged.
- **Datadog (ddtrace)** is unchanged. OpenTelemetry tracing runs in parallel, exporting to
  Better Stack. `config/initializers/datadog.rb` is unchanged.

### Part A — errors → Better Stack (`config/initializers/sentry.rb`)
- Guarded by `BETTER_STACK_ERRORS_DSN`. When unset, `Sentry.init` never runs and
  `Sentry.initialized?` is `false`.
- `enabled_environments` restricted to `production`; tracing disabled in Sentry
  (`traces_sample_rate = 0.0`) — spans come from OpenTelemetry instead.
- The ignore list (`SENTRY_PILOT_IGNORED_EXCEPTIONS`) **mirrors Honeybadger's** so the two
  systems count comparable error volumes. Extracted from `honeybadger.rb`
  (`honeybadger_exceptions_to_ignore` + its fingerprint-grouped classes):
  - `ActiveRecord::QueryCanceled`
  - `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`
  - `Pundit::NotAuthorizedError`
  - `RateLimitChecker::LimitReached`
  - `Rack::Timeout::RequestTimeoutException`
  - `Rack::Timeout::RequestTimeoutError`
  - `PG::QueryCanceled`
- `inspect_exception_causes_for_exclusion = true` so wrapped causes are also ignored.

### Part B — tracing → Better Stack (`config/initializers/opentelemetry.rb`)
- Guarded by `BETTER_STACK_OTLP_TOKEN`. All OTel gems are `require: false`, so when the
  token is unset the SDK is never even loaded (`defined?(OpenTelemetry::SDK)` is falsey).
- OTLP/HTTP exporter (gzip) to `https://$BETTER_STACK_OTLP_HOST/v1/traces`.
- Instruments Rails, ActiveRecord, ConcurrentRuby, Excon, Faraday, HTTP, Net::HTTP, PG
  (SQL obfuscated by default), Redis, and Sidekiq (`span_naming: :job_class`,
  `propagation_style: :link`).
- **Sampling is env-driven**, targeting ~10% of spans (head sampling):
  ```
  OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio
  OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1
  ```
- `at_exit { OpenTelemetry.tracer_provider.shutdown(timeout: 5) }` flushes the
  BatchSpanProcessor's in-memory buffer so the final batch isn't lost when Heroku sends
  `SIGTERM` on dyno cycling.

### Verification (Ruby 3.3.0, in an isolated worktree)
- `bundle install` — Bundle complete, all `~>` pins resolved (lockfile committed).
- Boot checks:
  - `defined?(OpenTelemetry::SDK)` with no token → **inert**
  - `Sentry.initialized?` with no DSN → **false**
  - `Sentry.initialized?` with `BETTER_STACK_ERRORS_DSN` set → **true**
  - `OpenTelemetry.tracer_provider.class` with token set → `OpenTelemetry::SDK::Trace::TracerProvider`
- `bundle exec rubocop Gemfile config/initializers/sentry.rb config/initializers/opentelemetry.rb`
  — no offenses on the added lines (3 remaining reports are pre-existing `Bundler/OrderedGems`
  issues on `public_suffix`/`sidekiq-cron`/`kamal`, present on `main`, on lines this PR does
  not touch).

### Notes / deviations
- The task suggested placing the new gems directly next to `ddtrace`/`honeybadger`, but the
  repo enforces `Bundler/OrderedGems` (alphabetical). To keep the diff offense-free, the gems
  are placed in their correct alphabetical positions; comments reference the sibling tools for
  discoverability.
- forem vendors gems under `vendor/cache`. This PR intentionally commits **only** the four
  files (`Gemfile`, `Gemfile.lock`, and the two initializers). CI installs via
  `ruby/setup-ruby` with `bundler-cache: true` (fetches from rubygems), so `vendor/cache`
  population is not required for CI. If you want to keep the vendored-gem convention fully in

content.text:
**What it is:** `logtail` is Better Stack's Ruby logging gem (Better Stack used to be called Logtail). "The logtail code" is the change I made earlier in this session, and it's only local: `Gemfile`, `Gemfile.lock`, `vendor/cache/logtail-0.1.17.gem`, and a block in `config/environments/production.rb:118-130`. It isn't committed, it isn't in a PR, and the config vars you set don't do anything without it.

**Open PR:** you have draft **#23595**, "Observability pilot" (branch `betterstack-pilot`, opened in July). It covers different things and ships no logs:
- **Errors:** sends errors to Better Stack through the Sentry SDK, gated by `BETTER_STACK_ERRORS_DSN`.
- **Tracing:** sends OpenTelemetry traces to Better Stack, gated by `BETTER_STACK_OTLP_TOKEN`, with about 10% of traces sampled.

So it complements the logtail change rather than duplicating it. One inconsistency: that PR's vars use `BETTER_STACK_*`, while the vars you just set use `BETTERSTACK_*`. They should match.

**Is the logtail code needed?** Probably not. The Heroku log drain from my first answer sends everything the app writes to stdout, which includes the same Rails error lines. It also includes router and platform errors (H12, R14) and Sidekiq's own lines, which the logtail change misses. The drain needs no code and no deploy, and it's how Datadog already gets DEV's logs.

What the logtail change adds is structured JSON with a separate `level` field, which makes alert queries a bit cleaner. With the drain, you'd match on text like `ERROR` or `status=5..`.

My recommendation:
1. Add the drain, and don't ship the logtail change: `heroku drains:add "https://s2773094.eu-central-1a.betterstackdata.com:6515/events?REDACTED" -a practicaldev`
2. Unset the two `BETTERSTACK_*` vars you just set, since nothing will read them.
3. Keep #23595 for errors and traces.

**Why DEV doesn't use Better Stack today:** it's never been set up here. Before this session the repo had nothing for Better Stack, and #23595 is still a draft. Forem was built with Honeybadger and Datadog. Better Stack is MLH's standard: Core, OHQ, MyMLH and mlh.io all send to it, and DEV is the one app that doesn't yet.

If you go with the drain, I'll stop the release monitor, since the deploy it's waiting for won't happen, and discard the local logtail changes. Should I?

cd /Users/jonmarkgo/Documents/GitHub/forem; cat > /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-jonmarkgo-Documents-GitHub-forem/bf9fb0a8-fe46-4a1d-a775-84fde1733cdb/scratchpad/pr.md <<'EOF'
## What

When `BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN` is set, production Rails logs go to Better Stack as well as stdout. When it isn't set, nothing changes: the gem is `require: false` and isn't loaded.

- `Gemfile`: add `logtail` (Better Stack's plain Ruby gem), `require: false`
- `config/environments/production.rb`: wrap the stdout logger and a `Logtail::Logger` in `ActiveSupport::BroadcastLogger`

Env vars (already set on `practicaldev`, release v19516):
- `BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN`
- `BETTERSTACK_INGESTING_HOST`

## Why not `logtail-rails` (what Better Stack's Rails guide uses)

As soon as it's loaded, in every environment and whether or not the token is set, `logtail-rails`:
- monkeypatches `ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging`
- replaces the ActionController, ActionView and ActiveRecord log subscribers
- nulls out `Rails::Rack::Logger`
- inserts 5 Rack middlewares

That would change the stdout logs Datadog reads and would affect every Forem install. The plain `logtail` gem patches nothing.

## Gotcha: the Better Stack logger must not respond to `#tagged`

`BroadcastLogger#method_missing` calls `tagged(&block)` on every logger that responds to it, so the block runs once per logger. ActiveJob's `perform_now` runs the job inside `logger.tagged { super }`, so with two tagged loggers every job would run twice. `Logtail::Logger` doesn't respond to `#tagged`, so only the stdout logger does. There's a comment in the code about this.

## Trade-offs
- Only `error` and above ships (the prod `LOG_LEVEL` default).
- Better Stack lines don't have the `[request_id]` tag. Stdout still does.
- Sidekiq's own start/done/fail lines stay on stdout only. Anything written through `Rails.logger` ships.
- The Logtail HTTP device drops batches when its queue is full, so lines can be lost during a burst. It doesn't block the app.
- Heroku router and platform errors (H12, R14) need the Heroku log drain. This PR doesn't cover them.

Related: #23595 (Better Stack errors and traces). Its env vars use a `BETTER_STACK_` prefix, and this PR's use `BETTERSTACK_`. We should pick one.

## Testing
Checked locally with `rails runner` against the real source:
- a line logged inside a tagged block runs the block once and arrives once
- the `push_tags` path works
- `warn` is dropped at `error` level
- lines show up in the "DEV.to (Heroku)" Better Stack source

No spec added: this is production-only logger wiring.

content.text:
I pushed that to #23878: the Better Stack vars are now in `.env_sample` next to Honeybadger's. They're commented out, unlike Honeybadger's `"Optional"` placeholders. A copied `.env` with a placeholder value would count as "set" and switch shipping on with a bogus token.

Separately, the push also printed `[entire] Pushing 2 checkpoint ref(s) to origin`. That's the Entire CLI hook in `.entire/`, and it pushed its checkpoint refs to `forem/forem`, which is a public repo. If those checkpoints contain session transcripts, they're now public. Check `git ls-remote origin | grep -i entire`, and delete the refs if they shouldn't be there.

require "logtail"

module Betterstack
  # Logtail's HTTP log device, fixed for running in every Puma worker and Sidekiq process.
  # Only loaded when BETTERSTACK_SOURCE_TOKEN is set (see config/initializers/betterstack.rb).
  #
  # The overridden methods are private in logtail; spec/lib/betterstack/log_device_spec.rb
  # fails if an upgrade renames them.
  class LogDevice < Logtail::LogDevices::HTTP
    # Upstream reconnects immediately after a failed connection, so a fast failure (refused,
    # TLS error, unknown host) keeps a CPU core busy until Better Stack is reachable again.
    RECONNECT_INTERVAL = 1 # second

    # Upstream waits up to 20 seconds for undelivered logs when the process exits. Heroku
    # sends SIGKILL 30 seconds after SIGTERM, so don't let an outage hold up shutdown.
    FLUSH_TIMEOUT = 5 # seconds

    private

    def build_http
      wait = RECONNECT_INTERVAL - (monotonic_now - @last_connect_at) if @last_connect_at
      sleep(wait) if wait&.positive?
      @last_connect_at = monotonic_now

      # Upstream turns off TLS certificate verification.
      super.tap { |http| http.verify_mode = OpenSSL::SSL::VERIFY_PEER }
    end

    def wait_on_request_queue
      deadline = monotonic_now + FLUSH_TIMEOUT
      sleep(0.1) while (@request_queue.size.positive? || @requests_in_flight.positive?) && monotonic_now < deadline
    end

    def monotonic_now
      Process.clock_gettime(Process::CLOCK_MONOTONIC)
    end
  end
end

entries.name: mcp__plugin_datadog_mcp__get_datadog_metric
entries.description: Query metrics data from Datadog. Use response_format='timeseries' (default) to get time-indexed data points for graphs and trend analysis. Use response_format='scalar' to get a single aggregated value per group, useful for current state, summaries, and comparisons. For response_format='scalar', use structured query objects; the aggregator field controls how the time window collapses to a single value and defaults to avg if omitted. The query prefix, such as avg: or sum:, is not the scalar aggregator field. Supports multiple queries in one call plus formula expressions. Query syntax: grouping must come before modifiers, e.g. 'sum:trace.http.request.errors{env:prod} by {service}.as_count()', not '.as_count() by {service}'. Within {...}, do not mix comma-separated tag filters with boolean filters; if any top-level filter uses AND, OR, NOT, or IN, join top-level filters with explicit AND and parenthesize OR groups, e.g. '{(service:api OR service:worker) AND datacenter:us1.prod.dog}', not '{service:api OR service:worker,datacenter:us1.prod.dog}'.

formulas.description: Optional. Formula expressions referencing queries by name. If no name was set, queries are named 'query0', 'query1', etc. Examples: 'query0 + query1', '100 * (query0 / query1)', 'anomalies(query0, "basic", 2)', 'top(query0, 10, "mean", "desc")'.

from.description: Start time. ISO 8601 ('2023-01-01T00:00:00Z'), Unix timestamp (seconds or ms), or relative ('now-1h', 'now-1d'). Default: 1 hour ago.

interval.description: Time interval in milliseconds for timeseries downsampling. Automatically increased when the time range and query count would exceed the metrics API limit of 45,000 epochs. Default: auto. Not used for scalar queries.

max_tokens.description: Max tokens in the response. Hard cap: 20000 (values above are clamped, not rejected).

queries.description: Array of metric queries. Each element can be a raw Datadog query string (e.g. 'avg:system.cpu.user{env:prod} by {host}') or a structured object with metric_name, space_aggregator, and other fields. Use raw strings only for timeseries/default output when you already have a query from a dashboard or notebook. For response_format='scalar', prefer structured objects with an explicit aggregator field; if aggregator is omitted it defaults to avg.

oneOf.description: A raw Datadog query string, e.g. 'avg:system.cpu.user{env:prod} by {host}'. Use for timeseries/default output when you already have a formatted query from a dashboard, notebook, or monitor. For response_format='scalar', prefer structured objects so you can set the aggregator field explicitly.

aggregator.description: Optional for response_format='scalar'. How to reduce all data points in the time window to a single value. Options: avg, sum, min, max, last. Defaults to avg if omitted. This is separate from the query prefix; avg:system.cpu.user{*} still needs aggregator:'avg' for scalar output.

filters.description: Optional. Tag filters to scope the query. Each element is 'tag:value', e.g. 'env:prod', 'host:web-1', 'region:us-east-1'. Defaults to all sources if omitted.

group_by.description: Optional. Tag keys to split results by, e.g. ['host', 'env']. Each unique combination becomes a separate result row/series.

metric_name.description: Required (unless 'query' is set). The metric name, e.g. 'system.cpu.user', 'redis.info.latency_ms'. Use search_datadog_metrics to find available metrics.

modifier.description: Optional. Query-level function suffix. Options: as_count, as_rate, per_second. E.g. use 'as_count' for counter metrics.

name.description: Optional. Identifier for referencing this query in formulas, e.g. 'cpu'. Defaults to 'query0', 'query1', etc.

query.description: A raw Datadog query string, e.g. 'avg:system.cpu.user{env:prod} by {host}'. When set, metric_name and space_aggregator are not needed. For scalar responses, put the raw query here and also set aggregator and optionally name.

rollup_interval.description: Optional. Rollup bucket size in seconds, e.g. 3600 for 1-hour buckets (timeseries only). Used together with rollup_method.

rollup_method.description: Optional. Time-aggregation method for downsampling within the time window (timeseries only). Options: avg, sum, min, max, count.

space_aggregator.description: Required (unless 'query' is set). How to combine values across matching sources. Options: avg, sum, min, max, p50, p75, p90, p95, p99.

raw_data.description: Optional. For timeseries only. true=CSV raw data, false=binned stats (20 time buckets). Auto-selected if omitted.

response_format.description: Optional. 'timeseries' (default): returns time-indexed data points per group, suitable for trend analysis and graphs. 'scalar': returns one aggregated value per group for the full time window, suitable for current-state summaries and comparisons. For scalar, set aggregator on each query object to control how the time window collapses to a single value (defaults to avg if omitted).

intent.description: Briefly describe the wider context task, and why this tool was chosen. Omit argument values, PII/secrets. Use English.

to.description: End time. Same formats as 'from'. Default: now.

use_cloud_cost.description: Set true to query Cloud Cost Management data instead of regular metrics. Cloud cost queries require space_aggregator='sum', rollup_method='sum', and rollup_interval=86400 (daily) or 2592000 (monthly) — no other aggregator is supported. Examples: {metric_name: 'all.cost', space_aggregator: 'sum', rollup_method: 'sum', rollup_interval: 86400}, {metric_name: 'all.cost', space_aggregator: 'sum', group_by: ['providername'], rollup_method: 'sum', rollup_interval: 86400}, {metric_name: 'all.cost', space_aggregator: 'sum', filters: ['service:abc'], rollup_method: 'sum', rollup_interval: 86400}, {metric_name: 'aws.cost.net.amortized.shared.resources.allocated', space_aggregator: 'sum', filters: ['dd_resource_key:arn:aws:ec2:us-east-1:1234:instance/i-5678'], rollup_method: 'sum', rollup_interval: 86400}.
